ranking_note: Authored from the before descriptions at commit dd26f634f41dfba929dc695f02eb4737a317bab3, frozen before the rewrite; protocol per /playbooks:skill-authoring ## Measurement. Same-plugin competitors only: mutation-testing:audit (running mutation analysis on a diff or the code changed tests exercise, and triaging the surviving mutants) and mutation-testing:setup (user-invoked: installing and configuring the ecosystem's mutation tool and the tracked config). principles owns explaining mutation-testing theory from the primary literature: what the score says beyond coverage, what mutant states and dispositions mean, operator choice, gating on the score, and the underlying hypotheses.

queries.request: Is mutation testing worth the CI time for a mid-size Python service, or is it mostly academic?
Explain, in terms of mutants, why 100% branch coverage doesn't mean the suite is strong.
What's an equivalent mutant, and why can't the tools just detect them automatically?
Where does the coupling effect come from, and does it hold for real-world bugs?
Which mutation operators give the most signal per mutant? Our tool enables dozens by default and runs take forever.
Why would Google suppress mutants in logging statements? What makes a node arid?
Our mutation score is stuck around 55% even though coverage is above 90%. What usually explains a gap like that?
Is it sensible to block merges on a minimum mutation score, or does that backfire in practice?
Quick one: what is the competent programmer hypothesis?
I need to explain to my manager what mutation testing measures that code coverage doesn't. Help me make the case.
Mutate the code changed in this branch and list the mutants that survive.
Set up PIT for our Gradle build and write the mutation config file.
This test asserts the mock was called twice. Is that check worth keeping, or should the expected value come from somewhere else?
Find tests in the repo that pass no matter what the code does.
Did my refactor actually reduce cyclomatic complexity? Compare against main.
Which parts of this change are riskiest and need new tests before merge?
Our coverage is high but I don't trust it. Break the payment code on purpose and see whether the tests notice.
Is mutation testing configured in this repo? The last mutation run fell back to defaults.
Is this snapshot-only test of the invoice renderer worth keeping?
Write property-based tests for the date parser so random inputs exercise the edge cases.
